newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: CZECH INDMIN SAYS CBANK SHOULD EASE MONEY POLICY.
newsitem.headline: CZECH INDMIN SAYS CBANK SHOULD EASE MONEY POLICY.

text.p: The Czech central bank should ease its monetary policy to spur economic growth and help state finances, Industry and Trade Minister Vladimir Dlouhy said on Thursday.

Speaking at a news conference, Dlouhy said the lowering of inflation should become a secondary target of Czech economic policy to helping the balance of payments and easing pressure on the state budget.

"The main target is to break the trends in payment balance and pressures which have been appering in the state budget. But we should not sacrifice economic growth, which will likely be slower than we expected in 1997," Dlouhy, an economist, told reporters.
"Inflation is only the last target. I am not saying we should not care about it at all, but it has dropped significantly, more than we were expecting," he added.

When asked if he thought the central bank should cut interest rates, Dlouhy replied: "Through this hierarchical organisation of targets I am indirectly answering your question," Dlouhy said. He did not elaborate.
Consumer prices rose 0.1 percent in March, putting the year-on-year inflation rate at an all-time low of 6.8 percent.

Concerns over the economy have been growing since industrial output figures showed a real decline in January and February, which analysts say is a result of CNB's restrictive policies imposed in mid 1996.

The government and the Czech National Bank (CNB) have been mulling a series of measures in order to help the slowing economy, stabilise foreign trade deficit, cut wage growth and bring state finances to balance.
On Thursday, the CNB announced it would lower minimum reserve requirements for banks to 9.5 percent from a previous 11.5 percent, though it did not touch interest rates.

The government said it would announce the measures after a regular meeting on April 16 and many analysts have said a rate cut may be in the cards if key M2 money figures expected this week are favourable.
Dlouhy declined to say what measures were under consideration, but warned against any irreversible action.

Some ministers have been pushing for an import surcharge as a cure for the trade deficit, but Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus said on Wednesday it was not on the agenda for next week as it would have to go through the parliament.
CNB governor Josef Tosovsky, once again, ruled out devaluation of the crown in a late Wednesday night interview with the Czech Television.

The state budget, approved as balanced with revenues at 549.1 billion crowns, showed an 8.5 billion deficit at the end of March. The foreign trade gap rose to 27.2 billion in February from 16.3 billion in January.
